t: The Enlightenment was a movement of writers, scientists and reformers who held that reason, evidence and free enquiry, not tradition or authority alone, should guide knowledge, belief and government.
Its thinkers, from John Locke and Voltaire to Adam Smith and Immanuel Kant, argued for toleration, natural rights, the rule of law, freer trade and the reform of cruel punishments.
Its ideas guided reforming monarchs and inspired the declarations of rights of 1776 and 1789, though the rights it proclaimed long excluded most women and the enslaved.
dyk: Émilie du Châtelet finished her French translation of Isaac Newton’s Principia, with a long commentary of her own, in 1749, the year she died; published complete in 1759, it is still the standard French version.
ev: Isaac Newton publishes the Principia, setting out the laws of motion and universal gravitation
John Locke publishes his Two Treatises of Government and An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
Montesquieu publishes The Spirit of the Laws, with its case for separating the powers of government
The first volume of the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d’Alembert, appears in Paris
Jean-Jacques Rousseau publishes The Social Contract and Emile; both are banned in France and Geneva
Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations; the American Declaration of Independence proclaims equal rights
Immanuel Kant answers the question “What is Enlightenment?” with the motto “Sapere aude”, dare to know
The French National Assembly adopts the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

f.where: Arose in England, the Dutch Republic and France; flourished in Paris, Edinburgh, Berlin, Königsberg, Milan and Naples, and spread to Spain, Portugal, Poland, Russia and the Americas
f.period: c. 1685–1815: from Newton’s Principia and Locke’s writings of the late 1680s to the end of the Napoleonic Wars; at its height between the 1740s and the 1780s
f.figures: John Locke, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Denis Diderot, David Hume, Immanuel Kant
f.outcome: Shaped modern science, liberal political thought, religious toleration and the idea of human rights; inspired the American and French revolutions and the reforms of “enlightened” monarchs
